```{r setup, message=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(GenomicRanges)
library(superintervalsr)
```

## Annotating peaks with genes

This small synthetic example demonstrates closed, end-inclusive genomic
coordinates. A map indexes one chromosome and ignores strand, equivalent to
`ignore.strand = TRUE` in the comparison below. Zero-width GRanges are not
supported. Use separate maps for distinct chromosomes.

```{r input}
genes <- GRanges(c("chr1", "chr1", "chr1", "chr2"),
                    IRanges(c(20, 1, 8, 1), c(30, 10, 18, 10)),
                    gene_id = c("GENE_C", "GENE_A", "GENE_B", "GENE_D"))
peaks <- GRanges("chr1", IRanges(c(5, 15, 25, 40), c(8, 22, 28, 45)))
chr1_rows <- which(as.character(seqnames(genes)) == "chr1")
chr1_genes <- genes[chr1_rows]
gene_map <- IntervalMap(chr1_genes, value_column = "gene_id")
counts <- count.batch(gene_map, start(peaks), end(peaks))
reference <- countOverlaps(peaks, chr1_genes, ignore.strand = TRUE)
stopifnot(identical(counts, reference))
mcols(peaks)$gene_count <- counts
peaks
```

## Retrieving source rows after indexing

`build()` sorts coordinates. Search indices refer to map positions, so they must
not be used directly to subset an unsorted or chromosome-filtered input.
Instead, retain original row IDs as values:

```{r row_ids}
row_map <- IntervalMap(start(chr1_genes), ends = end(chr1_genes),
                            values = chr1_rows)
row_ids <- unlist(search_values(row_map, 5, 22), use.names = FALSE)
genes[row_ids]
```

To return new genomic ranges containing the selected metadata column:

```{r conversion}
hits <- search_items(gene_map, 5, 22)
as_granges(hits, seqname = "chr1", valuename = "gene_id")
```

The conversion assigns the requested sequence name. It does not restore original
strand, sequence lengths, or metadata columns omitted when constructing the map.

## Set operations for covered regions and nearby features

```{r operations}
peak_map <- IntervalMap(peaks, value_column = "gene_count")
shared <- superintervalsr::intersection(gene_map, peak_map)
as_granges(search_items(shared, 1, 50), seqname = "chr1")

# Disjoint covered regions, and uncovered regions within a specified span.
merged <- superintervalsr::merge_overlaps(gene_map)
uncovered <- superintervalsr::gaps(merged, 1, 50)
as_granges(search_items(uncovered, 1, 50), seqname = "chr1")

# Clamped search windows; results are already indexed.
windows <- superintervalsr::expand(peak_map, 5, 5, lo = 1, hi = 50)
search_items(windows, 1, 50)
```

Intersection keeps the value of each left input interval and can emit overlapping
pieces. Merge and union keep one representative value per merged region; they
are coordinate operations, not an aggregation of all annotations. Adjacent
intervals without shared bases remain separate. Coverage sums intersection
widths with multiplicity:

```{r coverage}
superintervalsr::coverage(gene_map, 5, 10)
stopifnot(superintervalsr::coverage(gene_map, 5, 10)$total_coverage == 9)
```

## Repeated queries

Batch operations reduce R-to-C++ call overhead. Build once, query repeatedly,
and rebuild after additional intervals are added. The query path deliberately
does not check whether the index is up to date. Use valid whole-number query
ranges with start less than or equal to end. Compare correctness before
measuring
performance on data representative of your analysis:

```{r batch}
individual <- vapply(seq_along(peaks), function(i) {
        count(gene_map, start(peaks)[i], end(peaks)[i])
}, integer(1))
stopifnot(identical(individual, counts))
```
